enrichment.short_title: Whether unaccompanied asylum-seeking children accommodated by a local authority were looked-after children entitled to leaving-care duties
key_facts: Four unaccompanied asylum-seeking children arrived at Heathrow in 2000 destitute and were assisted by Hillingdon Social Services while aged 16 or 17 for periods well over 13 weeks.
As adults in further education, they claimed continuing duties under the Children (Leaving Care) Act 2000 as eligible and former relevant children.

Hillingdon contended they were not looked after because assistance was provided under section 17 rather than section 20 accommodation, and sought to read temporal limits into the eligible-child definition.
The council provided housing, subsistence and support services but argued a distinction between housing and statutory accommodation.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review by four claimants seeking declarations of eligibility under the leaving-care regime and priority-need homelessness status.
enrichment.outcome: All four applications succeeded; declarations granted that each claimant was an eligible child and is now a former relevant child, and in priority need for accommodation.
enrichment.ratio: Assistance given to lone children in need who require somewhere to live because no carer can provide suitable accommodation in the UK amounts to provision of accommodation under the Children Act 1989, so they were looked after within section 22(1)(b); the prescribed 13-week period in paragraph 19B need not begin before age 16, and housing provision cannot be distinguished from accommodation for these purposes.
legal_issues: Meaning of eligible child and former relevant child under the Leaving Care Act
Whether UASC assisted by social services were looked after under section 22 Children Act 1989
Whether accommodation provided under section 17 or section 20 affects leaving-care entitlement before November 2002 amendments
Construction of paragraph 19B(2)(b) prescribed period requirements

enrichment.short_title: Reduction of manifestly excessive two-year committal for breach of anti-social behaviour injunction
key_facts: A 19-year-old repeatedly breached a Middlesbrough Borough Council injunction excluding him from the Grove Hill Triangle area by dangerous motorbike riding and related conduct.
He had already served three months for an earlier breach and continued offending after release.
On 7 April 2003 he was arrested on unrelated matters, did not attend the committal hearing, and was committed in absentia for two years.
The committal notice was served only six clear days before hearing, contrary to the usual 14-day Practice Direction, but he had solicitors from 2 April.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal out of time against a county court committal order, limited to penalty after leave granted.
enrichment.outcome: Leave to appeal out of time granted on penalty only; appeal allowed to reduce committal from two years to nine months.
enrichment.ratio: The maximum two-year committal must be reserved for the worst cases; repeated breaches of an anti-social behaviour injunction by a young offender, though serious and persistent, did not justify the maximum sentence where the conduct did not involve personal violence or direct threats.
legal_issues: Whether Form N78 committal procedure complied with human rights requirements
Effect of non-compliance with the 14-day committal Practice Direction
Admissibility and weight of hearsay resident complaints
Appropriate length of committal for repeated injunction breaches

enrichment.short_title: Category A prisoner entitled to full disclosure of prison review reports under the Data Protection Act 1998
key_facts: Mr Lord, a life prisoner convicted of murder in 1981, remained Category A at HMP Frankland and sought full disclosure of annual Category A review reports rather than the anonymised gist normally provided.
The June 2001 gist presented staff views as unanimous, but underlying reports contained sharply conflicting recommendations on downgrade and escape risk.
After a section 7 request and complaint to the Information Commissioner, he issued proceedings seeking disclosure under the Data Protection Act 1998 and judicial review.
The Secretary of State resisted disclosure relying on exemptions and public interest, but the court read the reports and found the gist materially misleading.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review and Data Protection Act 1998 section 7(9) application following a Part 8 claim transferred to the Administrative Court.
enrichment.outcome: Application succeeded; claimant entitled in principle to full unredacted Category A reports under section 7(1), with discretion exercised in his favour under section 7(9).
enrichment.ratio: Category A reports are personal data to which a prisoner has a prima facie section 7(1) right of access; the Secretary of State failed to justify withholding under section 29(1), section 7(4) or section 8(2)(a), and where liberty interests are engaged the court should exercise section 7(9) discretion in favour of disclosure, especially where the gist did not fairly reflect conflicting report content required by ex p Duggan and ex p McAvoy.
legal_issues: Whether Category A prison reports are disclosable personal data under the Data Protection Act 1998
Application of sections 7, 8, 27, 29 and public-interest exemptions
Fairness of gist disclosure following ex p Duggan and ex p McAvoy
Exercise of discretion under section 7(9) where prisoner liberty is at stake

enrichment.short_title: Planning appeal dismissed over harmful rear housing terraces at Walton Road, Elmbridge
key_facts: Spa Properties appealed under section 288 against an inspector's dismissal of a planning appeal for redevelopment at Walton Road, Elmbridge.
The proposal included accepted flats on the Walton Road frontage and refused rear terraces of large three-storey-style houses set close to boundaries.
The inspector found harmful impact on character, appearance and residential amenity through overlooking and overbearing bulk despite compliance with local plan spacing guidance.
Bias was abandoned at hearing; six grounds challenged design assessment, screening, privacy and adequacy of reasons.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Section 288 appeal to the High Court against a planning inspector's decision on a refused housing scheme.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; inspector's refusal upheld and respondent costs assessed at £3,410.
enrichment.ratio: Planning judgments on design harm, effective storey height, loss of screening and perception of overlooking are matters for the inspector's planning judgment; mere compliance with development plan guidelines does not guarantee acceptable design, and the decision letter adequately explained why the proposed density and house types were unacceptable.
legal_issues: Whether the inspector mischaracterised roof-space accommodation as effectively three-storey development
Whether existing boundary screening and proposed landscaping were properly considered
Whether overlooking analysis including perception of loss of privacy was lawful
Whether reasons were adequate to guide a revised application

enrichment.short_title: Inspector wrongly excluded caravan use when deciding if barn was used as a dwellinghouse
key_facts: The appellant sought a lawful development certificate for residential use of a barn in Seed Road, Newnham, Kent Downs AONB, which contained two fitted-out caravans plus ancillary rooms.
Residential use had continued for more than four but less than ten years before the 2001 application, making the dwellinghouse versus caravan-use distinction decisive for immunity.
The inspector treated the caravans as not part of the building and assessed only non-caravan areas, finding insufficient domestic facilities for a dwellinghouse.
A linked enforcement notice decision depended on the LDC outcome and was accepted for remission if residential use was lawful.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Section 288 appeal against a second inspector's decision on a lawful development certificate, following quashing of an earlier decision.
enrichment.outcome: Inspector's decision quashed and remitted; permission to appeal against the enforcement notice granted and that appeal allowed; Secretary of State ordered to pay £4,776.60 costs.
enrichment.ratio: Use of caravans stationed within a building for residential purposes forms part of the use of the building when assessing whether its use is as a single dwellinghouse; it is wrong to treat physical non-integration of caravans as determinative and ignore their residential use in applying the Gravesham domestic-facilities test.
legal_issues: Whether stationing and residential use of caravans within a barn changed use to a single dwellinghouse
Application of section 171B four-year and ten-year enforcement immunity periods
Proper approach to Gravesham BC v SSE dwellinghouse test
Whether a remitted inspector must explain departure from an earlier quashed decision

enrichment.short_title: Six-day custody time limit extension upheld where judge lacked time for full hearing mid-trial

statutes_considered.title: Prosecution of Offences (Custody Time Limits) Regulations 1987

key_facts: Mr Walpole faced serious drug importation charges sent to Swindon Crown Court with a custody time limit due to expire on 29 August 2003.

On 27 August Judge McNaught, sitting in the middle of another trial without papers, initially declined to hear the extension application but later extended the limit by six days to 4 September for a half-day hearing.
Defence argued the statutory criteria in section 22(3) were not properly considered and that administrative convenience could not justify extension.
An agreed note of the hearing showed the judge extended time because insufficient time remained that day to deal with the application properly.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Urgent application for permission and substantive judicial review of a Crown Court custody time limit extension, heard together.
enrichment.outcome: Permission granted but application for judicial review dismissed; the short extension complied with section 22(3) and was not Wednesbury unreasonable.
enrichment.ratio: Even a very short custody time limit extension requires consideration of good and sufficient cause and due prosecution expedition, but where a judge extends time only to enable a proper contested hearing because he lacked preparation time during another trial, that can satisfy section 22(3) despite limited explicit reasons.
legal_issues: Whether section 22(3) criteria were applied before extending custody time limits
Whether administrative convenience can justify extension
Need for a fixed trial date, judge and court before extension
Priority to be given to liberty-related applications

enrichment.short_title: Chief Constable may be liable under section 41(2) Sex Discrimination Act for discriminatory acts of junior officers
key_facts: Detective Constable Angela Baskerville brought an employment tribunal claim against the Chief Constable of Kent for sexual harassment and sex discrimination by colleagues and supervisors at Margate.
The Chief Constable applied to strike out, relying on Chief Constable of Bedfordshire Police v Liversidge on race discrimination between officers.
The claim pleaded that officers acted as the Chief Constable's agents with his authority and that he failed to prevent harassment within his control.
The tribunal and EAT refused strike-out; the Chief Constable appealed on statutory construction of sections 17 and 41.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal with permission against Employment Appeal Tribunal refusal to strike out sex discrimination claim against a Chief Constable.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; claim remitted to the employment tribunal; permission to appeal to the House of Lords refused.
enrichment.ratio: Section 41(2) of the Sex Discrimination Act 1975 applies for the purposes of the whole Act, including section 17(1); where a police officer acts as agent of the Chief Constable with his authority in management or employment-related matters, the Chief Constable is treated as employer and may be liable for unlawful discrimination, subject to factual determination and excluding peace-officer acts covered by Farah.
legal_issues: Whether section 17(1) limits liability to acts personally done by the Chief Constable
Interaction between section 17 and section 41(2) Sex Discrimination Act 1975
Whether junior police officers can be agents of the Chief Constable for discrimination purposes
Appropriateness of strike-out where jurisdiction depends on disputed facts

enrichment.short_title: Magistrates rightly revoked section 35 hospital remand where NHS funding was not arranged
key_facts: Stephen B, a remanded defendant with PTSD and a history of violent conduct, consented to a section 35 remand to Ty Gwyn nursing home for psychiatric assessment on 13 June 2003.
Dr Jones advised Ty Gwyn was appropriate and said a bed was available subject to health authority funding, but Eden Valley Primary Care Trust refused funding after Dr Lamont recommended custody.
On 16 June magistrates revoked the section 35 order as ultra vires because section 35(4) required satisfied arrangements for admission within seven days, which funding refusal prevented.
The claimant remained in custody at Durham Prison pending Crown Court proceedings; parallel challenge to the PCT funding refusal was brought.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of magistrates' revocation of a section 35 hospital remand order and challenge to PCT refusal to fund Ty Gwyn placement.
enrichment.outcome: Application dismissed; magistrates were correct that the 13 June order was invalid without arranged admission, and funding declaration fell away; matter to proceed in Crown Court.
enrichment.ratio: Section 35(4) requires the court to be satisfied that admission arrangements to the specified hospital exist within seven days before making a hospital remand; confident medical expectation of future funding is insufficient, and where funding is absent the proper course is adjournment to resolve funding rather than make an ineffective order.
legal_issues: Construction of section 35(4) admission arrangements requirement
Whether Ty Gwyn was a hospital for section 35 purposes
Lawfulness of PCT refusal to fund a magistrates' section 35 order
Appropriate disposal where remand in custody may harm a mentally ill defendant

enrichment.short_title: No security order pending section 67 challenge to ICC award of group company losses
key_facts: C & M Farming obtained a London-seated ICC award of US$6.7 million against Peterson Farms for ALVJ virus in grandparent chicken stock supplied under an Arkansas-law contract.
About US$5.4 million represented losses of other group companies; Peterson challenged jurisdiction under section 67, contending the tribunal wrongly treated C & M as agent for the group.

C & M sought an unprecedented section 70(7) order securing the disputed award pending the section 67 application, pointing to post-award UCC financing statements and mortgages filed by Lloyd Peterson.
Peterson paid the undisputed portion and was pursuing enforcement and fraudulent-conveyance proceedings in Arkansas.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application under section 70(7) Arbitration Act 1996 for security pending a section 67 jurisdictional challenge to part of an ICC arbitral award.
enrichment.outcome: Application refused; court declined to order security for the disputed award amount.
enrichment.ratio: Section 70(7) should be exercised cautiously on as-of-right section 67 applications, especially where the jurisdictional challenge is not flimsy; the power protects against diminution of the losing party's ability to pay rather than improving the claimant's enforcement position, and here securing the award would effectively require the associated principal to fund a financially distressed company.
legal_issues: Scope of section 70(7) security pending section 67 jurisdiction challenges
Difference between section 67 challenges and sections 68/69 appeals
Whether post-award asset protection steps justified security
Whether the group-companies jurisdictional challenge lacked substance

enrichment.short_title: Custody time limit extension upheld after trial adjournment caused by defence change of solicitors

statutes_considered.title: Prosecution of Offences (Custody Time Limits) Regulations 1987

key_facts: Mr Taheri was remanded in custody from September 2002 on harassment and threats-to-kill charges, committed to Crown Court on 13 November 2002.
Trial fixed for 23 April 2003 was vacated when he changed solicitors on the eve of trial and relisted for 23 July 2003.
On 23 July the ten-day trial estimate could not be accommodated before Judge Burke's leave; custody time limits were extended to 18 September after a fixture on 15 September was obtained.
A later transcript showed counsel had not told the court on 23 April that the estimate had increased to ten days, so listing for 23 July was proper.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of Crown Court extensions of custody time limits under section 22(3), heard as permission and substantive hearing.
enrichment.outcome: Claim dismissed; Judge Burke lawfully extended custody time limits to 18 September 2003 on the facts as established.
enrichment.ratio: Listing unavailability caused by an increased trial estimate and defence-initiated change of representation can amount to good and sufficient cause under section 22(3), provided the prosecution acted with due diligence; administrative listing errors by court staff are not required where the true cause was defence failure to notify an amended estimate.
legal_issues: Whether unavailability of judge and courtroom is good and sufficient cause for extension
Effect of defence-initiated trial adjournment on custody time limits
Responsibility for notifying changed trial estimates to the court
Wednesbury review of Crown Court extension discretion
